Plowman
PLOW-man
noun
From plow (Saxon ploh, a ploughland) and man; the husbandman who drives the share through the ground. The Authorized Version spells it both plowman and plowmen, and the older English books freely ploughman.

Biblical Definition

The plowman is the man who breaks the ground for seed — the first labourer of the agricultural year and, in Scripture, a standing figure of patient, taught, hopeful work. Isaiah makes him a preacher: “Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?” (Isa 28:24). He ploughs a while and then sows, sets each seed in its appointed place, and threshes each grain with the instrument proper to it — “for his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him” (Isa 28:26). Every farmer’s good sense is a gift of common grace, and it images the discretion with which God deals with His own. When the heavens shut, the plowman is the first to be shamed: “Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads” (Jer 14:4). And when God turns the captivity of His people, the plowman is the measure of the blessing: “the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper” (Amo 9:13) — the harvest so long and so heavy that ploughing time comes round before the reaping is done. Isaiah promises that in the restored Zion strangers shall be their plowmen and vinedressers (Isa 61:5). Paul draws the ministerial lesson: “he that ploweth should plow in hope” (1Co 9:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

One who ploughs the ground; in Scripture the emblem of labour taught of God, ashamed in drought, and overtaking the reaper in the day of blessing.

expand to see more

PLOWMAN, one that plows or holds a plow; a husbandman; a cultivator of the ground; hence a rustic, a countryman.

From plow, Saxon ploh, a ploughland or measure of land, and man.

Hebrew charash, to cut or engrave, and so to plough; the participle is the plowman.

Isa 28:24–26 makes his measured method a parable of God’s instruction.

Amo 9:13 — “the plowman shall overtake the reaper”: a harvest that outruns the year.

Key Scripture

Isa 28:24 — "Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?"

Jer 14:4 — "Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads."

Amo 9:13 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt."

Isa 61:5 — "And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers."

Modern Corruption

Ordinary labour is treated as spiritually empty — a way to fund the real work rather than a calling in which God Himself instructs the workman to discretion.

expand to see more

A quiet error robs this word: the notion that manual, unremarkable, repetitive labour is at best neutral, a thing endured so that the important part of life can be paid for. Isaiah says otherwise about a man walking behind a plough in a field. The farmer’s knowledge of when to stop ploughing, what to sow where, which staff for the fitches and which cart wheel for the cummin — all of it, says the prophet, is because “his God doth instruct him to discretion, and doth teach him.” The competence of an honest workman is divine teaching. That is why Scripture can hand the plough back as a figure for the highest labour there is: he that ploweth should plow in hope (1Co 9:10), and no man having put his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God. The ploughman’s virtues — the straight furrow, the early start, the long patience between breaking ground and eating bread, the refusal to look behind — are the working Christian’s virtues, and they are learned in the field before they are named in the pulpit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is hope in the furrow. Jeremiah’s plowmen covered their heads because the ground was chapt and there was no rain; a man may break ground faithfully and see nothing come of it, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. But it sets against that the day the LORD promises through Amos, when the plowman shall overtake the reaper — the harvest so vast that the man coming to break ground for next year meets the man still gathering this year’s. That is what God intends for His labour in the earth. The minister who preaches into hard ground, the father who catechises children who do not seem to hear, the wife who prays for a husband year after year — all are plowmen, and all plow in hope, because the seed is not theirs, the rain is not theirs, and the day when the reaping outruns the ploughing has been promised by the mouth of the LORD.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The man who breaks the ground for seed; taught of God to discretion, ashamed in drought, and one day overtaking the reaper.

expand to see more

Plowman — plow (Saxon ploh, a ploughland) + man; Hebrew charash, to cut or plough.

Isa 28:24–26 — his measured method is a parable, and his discretion is taught him by God.

Jer 14:4 — in drought the plowmen are ashamed and cover their heads.

Amo 9:13 — the plowman overtakes the reaper when the LORD turns the captivity of His people.

1Co 9:10 — “he that ploweth should plow in hope”: the figure applied to gospel labour.

Usage

"The farmer’s plain competence is divine teaching: “his God doth instruct him to discretion.”"

"The plowman’s virtues — early start, straight furrow, long patience, no looking back — are the Christian’s."

"Plowmen ashamed in the drought and plowmen overtaking the reaper are the same men in two seasons."
